screens.title: Loading Data into Snowflake: Overview and Staging
screens.narratorSegment: This lesson introduces the staging layer — the temporary landing zone that makes Snowflake’s bulk loading fast and reliable. You will learn what a stage is, why Snowflake separates file upload from table insertion, and how that separation makes large-scale loading efficient. We’ll cover internal and external stages, the three kinds of internal stages you’ll encounter, and the client-side command you use to upload local files. For example, you’ll see how a simple CSV created on your laptop is uploaded to an internal named stage and then verified before being copied into a table. Understanding staging matters because it decouples transport from ingestion: you can validate, compress, and centralize files before the COPY step, which simplifies automation and troubleshooting. A common misconception is that INSERT statements are the normal way to bulk-load large files; in Snowflake, bulk-loading through stages is the designed pattern for parallel import. By the end of this chapter you’ll understand how to create a named stage, use the PUT command from your client machine, confirm uploads with LIST, and choose an appropriate file format. Think about one dataset you own and how staging could make its ingestion repeatable and auditable.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Overview & Staging
Loading Data into Snowflake
Understand staging, upload commands, and file formats for efficient bulk loads.
In this lesson
You will learn the role of stages, types of internal stages, how to create a named stage, the PUT and LIST commands, and file format considerations.
Why it matters
Staging decouples transport from ingestion so loads run in parallel, can be validated, and become automatable and auditable.
Quick orientation

Create a named stage, PUT your local file, LIST to confirm the upload, then COPY INTO the target table.

Visual Concept
Files travel from client → stage → table

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will master four practical skills that make staging and loading predictable and safe. First, you will explain why stages exist and how they separate file transfer from table ingestion; this helps you design reliable pipelines and debug loads without touching table data. Second, you will distinguish internal and external stages, understanding when to use Snowflake-managed storage versus referencing existing cloud buckets. Third, you will create and manage internal named stages and use the client-side PUT command to upload local files; this includes common path formats for Linux, Mac O S, and Windows. Fourth, you will recognize common file formats supported by Snowflake, and choose a format based on the structure of your source data. Each objective is practical: for instance, creating a named stage enables repeatable uploads across teams, while choosing Parquet or CSV affects performance and schema mapping. After studying these objectives you’ll be ready to stage a sample CSV from your laptop and verify it with LIST, which validates that your files were uploaded successfully.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practical Steps
screens.narratorSegment: These secondary objectives focus on concrete actions and verification steps you will be able to perform. You will create a practice database and schema for staging, which keeps practice work isolated and repeatable. You will craft the PUT command correctly for your operating system, including the required file URI prefix and the stage name. Finally, you will run LIST on the stage to confirm the presence of uploaded files and recognize the automatic compression that Snowflake applies. Practically, this means you can show a sample CSV uploaded from your desktop and demonstrate that the stage contains a compressed file. These actions are short but essential: they form the scaffolding for production pipelines where automation and monitoring rely on predictable staging behavior.

keyIdea.title: Practical skills
keyIdea.text: Create a practice schema and named stage, run PUT from your client, and use LIST to verify uploaded and compressed files.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Practical Steps
Setup for Practice
Create a practice database and schema to stage files safely.
CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS DATA_LOAD_DB;
USE DATABASE DATA_LOAD_DB;
CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS STAGING_SCHEMA;
USE SCHEMA STAGING_SCHEMA;
These statements isolate your practice work so uploads and stages do not affect production objects.
Create a Named Stage
Use CREATE OR REPLACE STAGE to define an internal named stage with an optional comment.
CREATE OR REPLACE STAGE my_customer_stage
  COMMENT = 'Internal stage for customer data files';
Named stages are schema objects and can be shared in role-based access patterns. They are preferred for team pipelines.
PUT command examples
Run PUT from your terminal (client-side). Note the file URI format differs by OS.
# macOS / Linux
PUT file:///Users/youruser/Desktop/sample_customers.csv @my_customer_stage;

# Windows
PUT file://C:/Users/youruser/Desktop/sample_customers.csv @my_customer_stage;
PUT runs on the client and uploads files to the Snowflake-managed internal stage, compressing them automatically.
Verification
Use LIST @my_customer_stage; to confirm uploaded files appear. Snowflake will often show the compressed filename with a .gz suffix.

screens.title: What is a Stage?
screens.narratorSegment: A stage is a temporary storage location that holds files before Snowflake loads them into tables. Think of it as a centralized landing area where you can validate, compress, and organize files so the COPY step can run in parallel and at scale. This two-step approach — upload to stage, then COPY INTO table — is central to Snowflake’s bulk-loading design. For example, imagine a marketing team produces daily CSV exports. Instead of running many INSERT statements, the team uploads the daily file to a stage, inspects or validates it, and then runs a COPY INTO command to ingest all rows in parallel. That structure reduces load times and prevents partial writes while you inspect data quality. A common misconception is to treat a stage like a permanent data store; stages are intended as transient or intermediate storage, not the authoritative source. However, named internal stages can be reused by teams for repeated uploads. In practice, staging improves observability and repeatability for pipelines. Reflect on a dataset you load now: could a staging step reduce rework and make ingestion easier to automate and monitor?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: A stage is an intermediary storage area where files are uploaded and validated before parallel loading into a table.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › What is a Stage?
Stage — a concise definition
Temporary landing zone for files before copy/ingest into tables.

Why use a stage: it decouples file transfer from table ingestion. That enables validation, compression, and parallel COPY operations that are much faster than row-by-row INSERTS.

Analogy
Files are like shipments dropped at a warehouse (stage) before being loaded into the factory (table).
Example
A daily customer export CSV is PUT to a stage, LISTed for verification, then COPY INTO the customers table.
Key Takeaway

Use stages to centralize and validate files before bulk ingestion to gain speed and auditability.

Common misconceptions
  • Stages are not long-term storage; they are intermediate landing zones.
  • Staging does not replace the need to validate schema and formats before COPY INTO.
  • INSERT is not a substitute for bulk loads when dealing with large files; use staging and COPY for scale.
Check your understanding
Describe a recent file you loaded and one benefit you would gain by adding a staging step before ingest.

screens.title: Internal vs External Stages
screens.narratorSegment: Internal and external stages solve the same basic problem — making files available to Snowflake — but they serve different operational needs. Internal stages are fully managed by Snowflake. That means you do not provision cloud storage or configure external permissions; Snowflake handles the storage, security via role-based access, and the upload lifecycle. Internal stages are convenient for ad-hoc uploads, small team pipelines, and learning environments. External stages reference files that already live in cloud storage like Amazon S3 or Azure Blob Storage. Use external stages when data already resides in a cloud bucket, when you need to maintain a separate data lake, or when governance and cost controls require using a single storage account. A common mistake is to assume external stages always improve performance; they can reduce egress or duplication when data is already external, but they require additional configuration such as storage integrations or IAM roles. For exam and practice focus on internal named stages first, then learn how external stages integrate with cloud permissions. Which setup best fits your team's ownership model: let Snowflake manage storage, or keep storage centralized under your cloud account?

keyIdea.title: Trade-off summary
keyIdea.text: Internal = Snowflake-managed simplicity; External = references external cloud storage for integration and governance control.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Internal vs External
Internal Stages
Managed by Snowflake; easy to create and use for uploads from your client.
  • No separate cloud storage to provision.
  • Access controlled by Snowflake roles and privileges.
  • Includes user, table, and named internal stages.
When to prefer
For quick team pipelines, teaching, and when you don’t want to manage external bucket permissions.
External Stages
Reference files in S3, Azure Blob, or GCS without copying them into Snowflake-managed storage.
  • Use when data already exists in cloud storage or when a centralized data lake is required.
  • Requires configuring cloud permissions, storage integrations, or IAM roles.
  • Saves duplication but adds configuration responsibility.
When to prefer
When governance or cost requires central cloud storage ownership and direct referencing of existing files.
Practical question

Do your files already live in a cloud bucket you control? If yes, an external stage avoids copying; if not, start with internal named stages for simplicity.

screens.title: Types of Internal Stages
screens.narratorSegment: Snowflake provides three internal stage types: user stages, table stages, and named internal stages. User stages are assigned per user and are useful for temporary, ad-hoc uploads. They are referenced using @~ and are convenient when a single user needs to upload and test files quickly. Table stages are tied to a specific table and are referenced using @%table; these are helpful when files are intended for a single table and you want a dedicated place for its incoming files. Named stages are schema-level objects you explicitly create with CREATE STAGE; they are the most flexible because multiple users or processes can write to and read from a single named stage. Named stages are commonly used in production pipelines where teams coordinate uploads and automate COPY steps. A frequent misconception is that table stages replace named stages; in reality, table stages are narrow and scoped while named stages serve team-level workflows. For hands-on practice, start by creating a named stage in a staging schema so you can practice PUT and LIST across sessions and users. Types of Internal Stages means user stages for individual workflows, table stages for per-table files, and named stages for reusable team pipelines.. In practical terms, user, table, and named stages — roles and uses. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: User stages for individual workflows, table stages for per-table files, and named stages for reusable team pipelines.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Types of Internal Stages
User Stage (@~)
Assigned per user for ad-hoc uploads.
Good for quick tests and single-user work where you don’t need shared access.
Example: a developer uploads a test CSV using their user stage to verify parsing rules before adding to a pipeline.
Table Stage (@%table)
Tied to a specific table and intended for that table’s incoming files.
Useful when files are produced specifically for one table and you want reduced namespace clutter.
Example: nightly export files for a single table are uploaded directly to its table stage for a nightly COPY job.
Named Stage (CREATE STAGE)
Schema-level stage created explicitly for shared access.
Preferred for pipelines where multiple users or services will read and write the same staging location.
Example: a named stage holds upstream partner files and is consumed by scheduled COPY jobs across multiple tables.
Misconception
Do not assume table stages scale for multi-team workflows. Use named stages when you need shared, repeatable access.

screens.title: Creating a Named Internal Stage
screens.narratorSegment: When you need a reusable staging location, create a named internal stage with CREATE OR REPLACE STAGE. This command defines a schema-level object and allows you to add a comment for team documentation. The named stage can be used by multiple users and automated jobs. For example, creating my_customer_stage with a comment makes intent clear and simplifies role-based privileges. After creating the stage, you can upload files using PUT from your laptop and reference the stage name in COPY INTO operations. A typical practice is to put the creation statement in your deployment scripts so the stage exists before automated processes run. A misconception is that CREATE STAGE needs cloud credentials for internal stages; it does not — Snowflake handles the storage. As you practice, include a clear comment and consistent naming to make it easy for colleagues to find and use the stage. keyIdea.text: Use CREATE OR REPLACE STAGE to make a schema-level internal stage and document it with COMMENT for team clarity.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Create Named Stage
CREATE OR REPLACE STAGE
Define a named internal stage and add a comment to document purpose.
-- Example: Creating an internal named stage
CREATE OR REPLACE STAGE my_internal_data_stage
  COMMENT = 'Stage for loading customer data';
Include this statement in deployment scripts so the stage exists for automated upload jobs.
Practical notes
  • Named stages are schema objects and follow RBAC rules for grants.
  • Use clear, descriptive names to help teams discover staging locations.
  • Comments serve as lightweight documentation for pipeline owners.
Key Takeaway

Create named stages for shared pipelines; include comments so the stage purpose is obvious.

screens.title: Uploading Files with PUT
screens.narratorSegment: The PUT command is how you upload local files to an internal stage. Important: PUT runs from your client machine or SnowSQL session and not inside the Snowflake warehouse. You must specify a file URI and the target stage. On Linux or Mac O S the URI begins with file:///, while on Windows you include the drive letter after file://. For instance, uploading sample_customers. csv from your desktop uses PUT file:///Users/youruser/Desktop/sample_customers. csv @my_customer_stage; on Windows you might use PUT file://C:/Users/youruser/Desktop/sample_customers. csv @my_customer_stage;. Snowflake automatically compresses files during PUT, which reduces storage and transfer time; you will typically see the uploaded filename with a. gz suffix when you LIST the stage. Common mistakes include incorrect file paths and forgetting the stage name. Always confirm the path exists on the client and that you have permission to read the file. After PUT succeeds, the stage contains the compressed file and is ready for COPY INTO operations. Try a small CSV first to verify your client-side path and syntax. keyIdea.title: PUT essentials
keyIdea.text: PUT runs on the client; use correct file URI syntax for your OS and confirm uploads with LIST. Files are compressed automatically.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Uploading with PUT
PUT: client-side uploads
Ensure the file path is correct and that you run PUT from the machine that has the file.
# macOS / Linux
PUT file:///Users/youruser/Desktop/sample_customers.csv @my_customer_stage;

# Windows
PUT file://C:/Users/youruser/Desktop/sample_customers.csv @my_customer_stage;
Note that PUT compresses files automatically, so you will often see sample_customers.csv.gz in the stage listing.
Common mistakes
  • Using an incorrect local path or relative path that doesn’t exist on the client.
  • Running PUT from a remote machine where the file is not present.
  • Forgetting to specify the target stage name after the file URI.
Pro tip
Test with a tiny CSV first. LIST the stage to confirm the compressed filename before attempting large uploads.

screens.title: Verify Uploads with LIST
screens.narratorSegment: After you run PUT, verify the upload with the LIST command. LIST @my_internal_stage; shows the files present in an internal stage and helps you confirm that the correct files arrived and were compressed. Typically, Snowflake will display the uploaded filename with a. gz suffix because PUT compresses files automatically. Use LIST to check file names, sizes, and timestamps; these metadata elements help you detect partial uploads and confirm freshness. A common misconception is that a successful PUT implies the file contents were validated; PUT only uploads and compresses — you still need to validate schema and data quality before or during the COPY step. For example, after PUT you might run LIST and then preview the file or run a staged COPY INTO a transient table for a quick schema check. Consistently listing and verifying staged files before automated COPY jobs reduces unexpected failures and makes pipelines more reliable. Ask yourself: when automating uploads, how will your process verify new files and signal readiness for ingestion? LIST command

screens.title: Supported File Formats
screens.narratorSegment: Snowflake supports multiple file formats for loading, and choosing the right format affects parsing, performance, and schema mapping. CSV is common for structured, tabular data and is easy to create from spreadsheets. JSON is for semi-structured records and suits nested or variable fields. Columnar formats like Parquet and ORC are efficient for large datasets and preserve schema and types, which can improve read performance and reduce storage. Avro and XML are also supported in scenarios where those systems are the source. When deciding, consider source fidelity and downstream queries: if you have nested objects, JSON or Parquet may preserve structure better than CSV. For simple flat records, CSV is sufficient and familiar. A misconception is to default to CSV for all cases — while it works, it can lose type information and be slower for very large datasets. In practice, take a small sample and confirm that your COPY INTO options match the format’s characteristics, such as field delimiter, header presence, and compression. Choosing the correct format makes loading predictable and efficient. screens.title: Security and Permissions for Stages
screens.narratorSegment: Security for staging revolves around access control. For internal stages, Snowflake uses role-based access control. Users need appropriate privileges such as USAGE on the stage and permission to read files in the stage. Granting only necessary rights follows the principle of least privilege and reduces accidental exposures. For external stages, you must also configure cloud-side permissions so Snowflake can access your external bucket; this usually involves setting up storage integrations or IAM roles depending on the cloud provider. A common mistake is granting overly broad cloud permissions or forgetting to restrict who can list or read staged files. For practice, grant USAGE to a specific role and test operations from that role; verify that unauthorized roles cannot access the stage. Document your stage access policy so automation and people both use the same secure pattern. In short, internal stages keep storage management inside Snowflake while external stages require coordination with cloud identity and access management. Security and Permissions for Stages means use rbac for internal stages and configure cloud permissions carefully for external stages; prefer least privilege for all access.. In practical terms, rbac for internal stages and external permissions for cloud buckets. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: End-to-End Staging Workflow
screens.narratorSegment: A reliable staging workflow follows a predictable sequence: prepare, upload, verify, and ingest. First, prepare your file and environment — create a practice database, schema, and a named stage if needed. Second, upload the file with PUT from the client machine that holds the file. Third, verify the upload using LIST; confirm the compressed filename, size, and timestamp so you can detect mistakes early. Fourth, perform any validation steps you require, such as copying into a transient table for schema checks or running small parsing queries on staged semi-structured files. Finally, perform the COPY INTO target_table to ingest the data for production use. This separation of steps reduces the blast radius of failures because you can validate files before they touch production tables. A common misconception is to skip verification and run COPY immediately; that can lead to partial or wrong loads. By following this staged workflow you gain repeatability, clearer troubleshooting, and easier automation. Consider scripting these steps so your CI/CD pipeline enforces verification before ingestion. End-to-End Staging Workflow means prepare environment, put files, list to verify, validate contents, then copy into target tables for ingestion.. In practical terms, from local file to table — the recommended sequence. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. screens.title: Common Mistakes and Pro Tips
screens.narratorSegment: When staging and uploading, several recurring pitfalls can slow you down. First, file path errors are frequent: ensure you run PUT from the machine that actually contains the file and verify the URI syntax for your operating system. Second, permission gaps occur when roles lack USAGE or when external stages lack the proper cloud permissions; test permissions by switching roles or using a minimal cloud role. Third, format mismatches happen when COPY INTO settings do not match your file (for example, wrong delimiter or header settings). To avoid these, always test with a small sample file and LIST the stage to check the compressed filename and size. Pro tips: use descriptive stage names and comments so team members discover intent, script the CREATE STAGE step in deployments, and use LIST as an automated verification step in CI. Another useful tip is to COPY INTO a transient table first for a quick schema validation before touching production tables. These small precautions make staging robust and reduce errors during scheduled loads. fullNarratorScript:
This lesson introduces the staging layer — the temporary landing zone that makes Snowflake’s bulk loading fast and reliable. You will learn what a stage is, why Snowflake separates file upload from table insertion, and how that separation makes large-scale loading efficient. We’ll cover internal and external stages, the three kinds of internal stages you’ll encounter, and the client-side command you use to upload local files. For example, you’ll see how a simple CSV created on your laptop is uploaded to an internal named stage and then verified before being copied into a table. Understanding staging matters because it decouples transport from ingestion: you can validate, compress, and centralize files before the COPY step, which simplifies automation and troubleshooting. A common misconception is that INSERT statements are the normal way to bulk-load large files; in Snowflake, bulk-loading through stages is the designed pattern for parallel import. By the end of this chapter you’ll understand how to create a named stage, use the PUT command from your client machine, confirm uploads with LIST, and choose an appropriate file format. Think about one dataset you own and how staging could make its ingestion repeatable and auditable.

In this chapter you will master four practical skills that make staging and loading predictable and safe. First, you will explain why stages exist and how they separate file transfer from table ingestion; this helps you design reliable pipelines and debug loads without touching table data. Second, you will distinguish internal and external stages, understanding when to use Snowflake-managed storage versus referencing existing cloud buckets. Third, you will create and manage internal named stages and use the client-side PUT command to upload local files; this includes common path formats for Linux, Mac O S, and Windows. Fourth, you will recognize common file formats supported by Snowflake, and choose a format based on the structure of your source data. Each objective is practical: for instance, creating a named stage enables repeatable uploads across teams, while choosing Parquet or CSV affects performance and schema mapping. After studying these objectives you’ll be ready to stage a sample CSV from your laptop and verify it with LIST, which validates that your files were uploaded successfully.

These secondary objectives focus on concrete actions and verification steps you will be able to perform. You will create a practice database and schema for staging, which keeps practice work isolated and repeatable. You will write the CREATE OR REPLACE STAGE statement to create a named stage and understand the optional COMMENT clause for documentation. You will craft the PUT command correctly for your operating system, including the required file URI prefix and the stage name. Finally, you will run LIST on the stage to confirm the presence of uploaded files and recognize the automatic compression that Snowflake applies. Practically, this means you can show a sample CSV uploaded from your desktop and demonstrate that the stage contains a compressed file. These actions are short but essential: they form the scaffolding for production pipelines where automation and monitoring rely on predictable staging behavior.

A stage is a temporary storage location that holds files before Snowflake loads them into tables. Think of it as a centralized landing area where you can validate, compress, and organize files so the COPY step can run in parallel and at scale. This two-step approach — upload to stage, then COPY INTO table — is central to Snowflake’s bulk-loading design. For example, imagine a marketing team produces daily CSV exports. Instead of running many INSERT statements, the team uploads the daily file to a stage, inspects or validates it, and then runs a COPY INTO command to ingest all rows in parallel. That structure reduces load times and prevents partial writes while you inspect data quality. A common misconception is to treat a stage like a permanent data store; stages are intended as transient or intermediate storage, not the authoritative source. However, named internal stages can be reused by teams for repeated uploads. In practice, staging improves observability and repeatability for pipelines. Reflect on a dataset you load now: could a staging step reduce rework and make ingestion easier to automate and monitor?

Internal and external stages solve the same basic problem — making files available to Snowflake — but they serve different operational needs. Internal stages are fully managed by Snowflake. That means you do not provision cloud storage or configure external permissions; Snowflake handles the storage, security via role-based access, and the upload lifecycle. Internal stages are convenient for ad-hoc uploads, small team pipelines, and learning environments. External stages reference files that already live in cloud storage like Amazon S3 or Azure Blob Storage. Use external stages when data already resides in a cloud bucket, when you need to maintain a separate data lake, or when governance and cost controls require using a single storage account. A common mistake is to assume external stages always improve performance; they can reduce egress or duplication when data is already external, but they require additional configuration such as storage integrations or IAM roles. For exam and practice focus on internal named stages first, then learn how external stages integrate with cloud permissions. Which setup best fits your team's ownership model: let Snowflake manage storage, or keep storage centralized under your cloud account?

Snowflake provides three internal stage types: user stages, table stages, and named internal stages. User stages are assigned per user and are useful for temporary, ad-hoc uploads. They are referenced using @~ and are convenient when a single user needs to upload and test files quickly. Table stages are tied to a specific table and are referenced using @%table; these are helpful when files are intended for a single table and you want a dedicated place for its incoming files. Named stages are schema-level objects you explicitly create with CREATE STAGE; they are the most flexible because multiple users or processes can write to and read from a single named stage. Named stages are commonly used in production pipelines where teams coordinate uploads and automate COPY steps. A frequent misconception is that table stages replace named stages; in reality, table stages are narrow and scoped while named stages serve team-level workflows. For hands-on practice, start by creating a named stage in a staging schema so you can practice PUT and LIST across sessions and users. Types of Internal Stages means user stages for individual workflows, table stages for per-table files, and named stages for reusable team pipelines.. In practical terms, user, table, and named stages — roles and uses. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. Snowflake supports multiple file formats for loading, and choosing the right format affects parsing, performance, and schema mapping. CSV is common for structured, tabular data and is easy to create from spreadsheets. JSON is for semi-structured records and suits nested or variable fields. Columnar formats like Parquet and ORC are efficient for large datasets and preserve schema and types, which can improve read performance and reduce storage. Avro and XML are also supported in scenarios where those systems are the source. When deciding, consider source fidelity and downstream queries: if you have nested objects, JSON or Parquet may preserve structure better than CSV. For simple flat records, CSV is sufficient and familiar. A misconception is to default to CSV for all cases — while it works, it can lose type information and be slower for very large datasets. When staging and uploading, several recurring pitfalls can slow you down. First, file path errors are frequent: ensure you run PUT from the machine that actually contains the file and verify the URI syntax for your operating system. Second, permission gaps occur when roles lack USAGE or when external stages lack the proper cloud permissions; test permissions by switching roles or using a minimal cloud role. Third, format mismatches happen when COPY INTO settings do not match your file (for example, wrong delimiter or header settings). To avoid these, always test with a small sample file and LIST the stage to check the compressed filename and size.
